newsitem.title: JAPAN: Foreigners seen more wary in Japan stocks in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners seen more wary in Japan stocks in 1997.

text.p: Foreign investors, often a driving force in long-term rallies on the Japanese stock market, are likely to turn more cautious in 1997, analysts say.
The yen's weakening against the dollar cuts the dollar-denominated value of Japanese equities, which may send the yen and stocks down into a double short term spiral, they say.

But foreign investors are expected to resume buying of stocks later next year, helped by a rising trend on Wall Street and pressures to increase holdings of Japanese equities due to their global asset allocation strategies.
"The double spirals (of falls in the yen and stocks) will likely continue in January, and the Nikkei could dive below 19,000 again," said Haruyoshi Mabuchi, chief strategist at Nikko Research Center.

On December 26, the Nikkei average of 225 leading issues tumbled more than 700 points, or 3.5 percent, to 18,819.92 at one stage, before bouncing back moderately. Overseas investors have been away from markets for extended Christmas holidays.
The Nikkei 225 was already below its low for 1995 on a dollar basis, which was $169.87. This could prompt foreign investors' sales to cut currency losses, he said.

But Mabuchi also said the focus in the market was currently on the government's economic policies and that investors were likely to resume buying when they became surer of a recovery in the economy in the latter half of 1997.
"You are not going to see the kind of buying that you've seen in the last couple of years. It will slow down," said Jeff Bahrenburg, Japan equity strategist at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.

Foreign investors' holdings of Japanese equities surged by 15 trillion yen ($130 billion) to 40 trillion yen in the year that ended in March. This was 10.5 percent of all investors' holdings, a record high ratio, the Tokyo Stock Exchange said.
Bahrenburg also said the market could see foreign investors' selling continue in the short term in 1997.
But "people feel that the market is oversold and has under-performed so much, so lots of asset allocation pressures put a little more money in Japan", he added.
The money inflows from overseas would be supported by a rally in European and U.S. stock markets, he said.

Kiyoshi Kimura, head of research at Societe Generale Securities Ltd, said overseas investors would cut the weighting of Japanese stocks in their portfolios in 1997, depressed by a lack of government steps to speed up economic growth.
"They will probably be net buyers, but they are going to reduce the weighting of Japanese equities," he said.
"Japan's economy is not in a situation where people can be very optimistic. The yen is high for the huge budget deficits, and investors can't buy stocks in such a country," he added.
Many analysts said one of the factors to trigger foreign investors' buying next year would be a tougher government stance to step up deregulation and support economic recovery.
Earlier in December, Tokyo stocks were battered by worries about the effects on the economy of the government's tightening of fiscal policy to tackle Japan's budget deficit.

The government has decided to end special income tax cuts from January and raise the consumption tax next April, sparking fears in the market that a fledgling recovery in the economy may be damaged. ($1=115 yen)
